architectureFigure.caption: Training procedure of GAD. The student (generator) learns to generate responses that maximize the score assigned by the discriminator. The discriminator is trained with Bradley-Terry loss to assign a lower score to the student than the teacher, learning to distinguish between them. Together, they form a two-player minimax game in an adversarial learning framework.

authors: Tianzhu Ye, Li Dong, Zewen Chi, Xun Wu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei

breakthroughAssessment.justification: The paper presents GAD, a novel and effective framework for black-box LLM distillation that addresses key challenges of on-policy learning without access to teacher logits. By framing distillation as a minimax game with an adaptive discriminator, GAD overcomes the limitations of prior black-box and on-policy methods, demonstrating robust performance, superior generalization, and resistance to reward hacking. The approach significantly advances the state-of-the-art for black-box distillation, especially for proprietary models.

coreProblem.concreteExample: When a proprietary API model (e.g., GPT-5) serves as the teacher, its internal states or logit distributions are inaccessible, making white-box distillation methods unfeasible. Extending on-policy learning to this black-box setting is challenging due to the lack of probability-level supervision signals for student-generated responses.
coreProblem.statement: Black-box distillation trains a student model using only the textual outputs of a teacher, without access to its internal logits or parameters. The absence of fine-grained probability supervision makes conventional likelihood-based objectives unavailable, and on-policy learning without explicit feedback on the quality of student generations is infeasible.
whyItMatters: Enables creation of smaller, more efficient student models from larger, resource-intensive proprietary teacher models without internal access.
Overcomes the limitations of white-box distillation methods when teacher models are proprietary APIs or closed-source.
Facilitates on-policy learning, which promotes mode-seeking behavior and reduces exposure bias, in the challenging black-box setting.

evaluationHighlights: GAD consistently surpasses SeqKD and instruction models without distillation across various LLM sizes and datasets (GPT-4o scores).
Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct distilled with GAD achieves performance comparable to the proprietary GPT-5-Chat teacher on the LMSYS-Chat benchmark.
GAD demonstrates strong improvements in out-of-distribution generalization, where SeqKD often performs poorly, sometimes yielding negative gains.
Human evaluations validate GAD's superiority with high win rates (exceeding 50%) and low loss rates (below 30%) against baselines.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of warmup strategies, Bradley-Terry loss, and balanced generator-discriminator sizes for optimal performance, and GAD's resistance to reward hacking.

mainTakeaways: GAD consistently outperforms the instruct model before distillation and the SeqKD baseline across all datasets and model variants in automatic evaluation (GPT-4o scores).
GAD shows particularly strong gains in out-of-distribution generalization compared to SeqKD, which often yields marginal or negative improvements.
On GPT-4o score, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct distilled with GAD approaches the capability of the GPT-5 teacher itself.
Human evaluations confirm GAD's superiority, achieving win rates exceeding 50% and loss rates below 30% against baselines.
SeqKD tends to overfit to local patterns, while GAD captures global stylistic characteristics and learns reachable modes, leading to better generalization.
The on-policy discriminator in GAD is stable and robust against reward hacking over thousands of training steps, unlike off-policy discriminators.

explanation: GAD frames the student LLM as a generator and trains a discriminator to distinguish its responses from the teacher LLM's, establishing a minimax game for black-box distillation.

The discriminator acts as an on-policy reward model that continually updates and co-evolves with the student, providing stable and adaptive feedback, which differs from fixed reward models in conventional RLHF.

This adversarial process provides implicit feedback on the quality of student generations without needing access to the teacher's internal probability space, addressing a major challenge in black-box on-policy learning.
The framework demonstrates robustness against reward hacking, a common issue observed in off-policy discriminator approaches for distillation.
keyNovelty.main: Introducing Generative Adversarial Distillation (GAD), a novel framework for black-box LLM distillation that enables on-policy learning without access to teacher logits or internal states by employing a generator-discriminator minimax game.

keyTerms.definition: A technique to transfer capabilities from a larger, resource-intensive teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student model.
A setting where the student model only has access to the teacher's text outputs, without access to internal logits or parameters.
Learning where the student learns from its own generated responses rather than solely imitating the teacher's outputs.
A framework where a generator and a discriminator compete in a minimax game to produce realistic data.
A probabilistic model for paired comparisons, used here to capture pairwise preferences between teacher and student responses for discriminator training.
A common black-box distillation method that performs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher responses.
A phenomenon in reinforcement learning where an agent exploits flaws in the reward function to achieve high scores without actually performing the desired task.

comparisonToPriorWork: Traditional white-box distillation methods (e.g., KLD, inner state matching) are inapplicable in the black-box setting due to lack of access to teacher internal states or logits.

Standard black-box distillation methods like Sequence-level Knowledge Distillation (SeqKD) perform supervised fine-tuning on teacher responses, which tends to memorize local lexical patterns and can overfit, leading to poor generalization.

Unlike conventional RLHF which trains a fixed reward model on a static dataset, GAD's discriminator acts as an on-policy reward model that continually updates and co-evolves with the student, providing adaptive feedback.
GAD's on-policy discriminator is robust against reward hacking, a common issue where off-policy discriminators can lead to agents exploiting flaws (e.g., producing excessively long responses).
GAD enables effective on-policy learning in the black-box setting, a challenge prior on-policy distillation methods faced due to the requirement for probability-level supervision.

modeling.label: Minimax Objective
modeling.value: $\max_G \min_D V(G, D) = E_{(x,y_t) \sim T} [-\log \sigma (D(y_t) - D(G(x)))]$ where $\sigma(\cdot)$ is the sigmoid function.

modeling.label: Discriminator Objective
modeling.value: $(Discriminator) \min_D E_{(x,y_t) \sim T} [-\log \sigma (D(y_t) - D(G(x)))]$ using Bradley-Terry loss.

pipelineFlow: The student LLM is framed as a generator G, which produces responses $G(x)$ for a given prompt $x$.
A discriminator D is trained to distinguish between teacher responses $y_t$ and student responses $G(x)$.
The generator G is optimized to produce responses that the discriminator cannot distinguish from those of the teacher, forming a two-player minimax game.
The discriminator acts as an on-policy reward model, continually adapting to the student's behavior during training.

A warmup stage is performed where both generator and discriminator are pre-trained for one epoch using cross-entropy loss (for generator) and Bradley-Terry loss (for discriminator) on teacher responses.

During the GAD training stage, the generator is updated using $D(G(x))$ as a reward signal via reinforcement learning (GRPO), and the discriminator is updated with Bradley-Terry loss to distinguish teacher responses $y_t$ from student responses $G(x)$.

problemDefinition.label: Teacher Distribution
problemDefinition.value: A teacher model $p(y|x)$ generates responses $y_t$ conditioned on a prompt $x$. In black-box distillation, only $y_t$ is observable, not $p(y|x)$.

problemDefinition.label: Student Model
problemDefinition.value: A student model $q_{\theta}(y|x)$ parameterized by $\theta$ aims to approximate the teacher's generative behavior.

problemDefinition.label: Black-box Setting
problemDefinition.value: The student has no access to the teacher's internal probability distribution or hidden states, only text outputs.

technicalDetails.reproducibility: Code and project page are available at aka.ms/GAD-project and aka.ms/GAD-github. Training details, including batch size, optimization steps, PPO mini-batch size, context length, and temperature are provided. Evaluation protocols and GPT-4o prompting are detailed.

systemModules.details: Generates responses $G(x)$ to prompts $x$. Optimized via policy gradient (GRPO) to maximize rewards provided by the discriminator.
systemModules.name: Generator (Student LLM)
systemModules.role: Student model that learns to imitate the teacher.

systemModules.details: Assesses the quality of student and teacher responses, distinguishing between them. Predicts a sequence-level scalar score $D([x,y])$. Trained with Bradley-Terry loss to assign higher scores to teacher responses ($D(y_t)$) than student responses ($D(G(x))$), co-evolving with the student.
systemModules.name: Discriminator
systemModules.role: Provides implicit, on-policy reward signal to guide student optimization.

thesis: Generative Adversarial Distillation (GAD), a framework that frames the student LLM as a generator and trains a discriminator to distinguish its responses from the teacher, enables effective on-policy and black-box distillation of large language models, consistently outperforming sequence-level knowledge distillation and achieving strong generalization.
title: Black-Box On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models
